books.section: Topic 7.4 The Progressives — The Progressive Movement
The Progressive Era and World War I (1900-1920)

primary_sources: Jacob Riis, How the Other Half Lives (1890)

stimulus.source_note: Verbatim excerpt (abridged) from Jacob Riis, How the Other Half Lives (1890), public domain.
stimulus.text: Here is the case of a woman employed in the manufacturing department of a Broadway house. ... She averages three dollars a week. ... lunch she cannot afford. One meal a day is her allowance. ... Almost any door might seem to offer welcome escape from such slavery as this. — Jacob Riis, How the Other Half Lives, 1890 (abridged)

source: original; stimulus paraphrased from 5 Steps to a 5 2024, Chapter 20, and Barron's Premium 2027, Chapter 9
stem: Riis's word 'slavery' most directly recalled the rhetoric of

options.misconception: Planters defended slavery as a good; they never used the word to condemn factory labor.

options.text: antebellum labor activists who denounced 'wage slavery'

options.misconception: Confederate generals fought to preserve slavery, not to condemn low wages.

options.text: abolitionists defending the Fugitive Slave Act
options.misconception: Abolitionists attacked the Fugitive Slave Act; they never defended it.

rationales.A: Planters praised slavery and claimed their workers were better off than factory hands. They never used 'slavery' to condemn a factory.
rationales.B: Antebellum labor activists, including the Lowell mill women, called industrial exploitation 'wage slavery.' Riis borrows their exact metaphor to condemn a woman's three-dollars-a-week life.
rationales.C: Confederate generals defended slavery as an institution. The metaphor of wage slavery belonged to its critics in the labor movement.
rationales.D: Abolitionists attacked the Fugitive Slave Act. Riis's metaphor comes from labor rhetoric, not from abolitionism.
rationales.general:
1. Read the metaphor. Riis calls a starving factory woman's life 'slavery,' and the word is doing argumentative work.
2. Ask who used that word that way before. Antebellum labor activists denounced low wages as 'wage slavery.'
3. Rule out the defenders. Planters and Confederates defended slavery, and abolitionists attacked the Fugitive Slave Act.
Remember: a metaphor's source matters, so ask who used the same words first and for what purpose.
